activity: building a project for the school science fair
knowledge_domain: building a project for the school science fair
fact: Repeating an experiment several times and averaging the results reduces the effect of random errors in any single trial.
story:
Peyton set the model catapult on the counter at the back of Ms. Bouchard's science classroom and pulled the release lever. The ping-pong ball sailed over the sink, bounced off the window, and rolled under Carlos's chair. Carlos held up his stopwatch. "Four meters, sixty centimeters. That's your launch distance."

"That can't be right," Peyton said. Yesterday in her driveway the ball had barely cleared two meters, and her data table was due at the science fair on Friday. She thought about the moment in class last week when Ms. Bouchard had dropped a crumpled paper ball three times to show how each drop landed slightly differently; the paper was the same, but the landings were not. Peyton had a feeling the same thing was happening here, though she couldn't see any reason for it.

"Hand me the ball," she said, in her most assertive voice. "We're running it ten times." She tugged the folder of graph paper out of her backpack, where she kept everything for the project because the economy of using one folder instead of four meant she never lost her notes. On the top page she wrote a note to herself in block letters: "Dear Friday Peyton, do not trust one launch. Do ten. Then average. Love, Tuesday Peyton." She read it back, decided it counted as a message, and got to work.

Launch one went wild again, all the way to the radiator. Launch two barely reached the edge of the counter. Carlos called out each number while Asia recorded them, and Peyton reloaded the lever every time without changing anything. "These numbers are all over the place," Asia said. "Does that imply your catapult is broken?"

"No," Peyton said. "It implies any single one of them could be wrong. But if I average ten, the wild ones stop mattering so much." She added the column of numbers, divided by ten, and wrote the answer at the bottom: three meters, twelve centimeters. She looked at it, then at her catapult, which had seemed so unreliable a minute ago.

"Steady number," she said. "Now we have something we can actually put on the board."

activity: to solve two-step equations and plot the line they describe on a coordinate grid
knowledge_domain: to solve two-step equations and plot the line they describe on a coordinate grid
fact: The x and y axes split the coordinate grid into four quadrants, numbered one to four going counterclockwise, starting from the top right.
story:
Emile slid his equation across the table so Solomon could see it. y = 2x minus 4. He had solved it for x = 3, x = 0, and x = negative 2, and now three points sat on his coordinate grid like tiny buoys. Math club had a contest going: whoever plotted the most correct points before the timer went off won a pass to skip one homework problem. Merrick was already on his fifth point, and the timer showed four minutes.

"Check this one," Emile said, tapping the point for x = negative 2, which gave y = negative 8. "It goes left and down. But look, Merrick's point at negative 1 and 5 goes left and up. And Solomon's at 6 and negative 3 goes right and down." He paused, pencil hovering. Was there some order to where things landed? The two axes cut the grid apart like streets slicing a neighbourhood, and every point seemed to belong to one particular block.

Solomon leaned over the empty grid printed in the back of Mr. Wang's practice packet. "Mr. Wang calls those sections quadrants," he said. "He had us label them last year." Emile studied the packet's small diagram. Quadrant one sat in the top right, where x and y were both positive. Then it went counterclockwise: quadrant two at top left, quadrant three at bottom left, quadrant four at bottom right, numbered one to four all the way around.

So his point at negative 2 and negative 8, both negative, lived in quadrant three. Merrick's was in quadrant two. Emile tested a hypothetical point in his head, something like x = 5 and y = negative 10, and traced it: right for the positive x, down for the negative y. That had to be quadrant four. It was like a rule hiding underneath the grid the whole time, and now that he could see it, he couldn't stop seeing it.

The timer beeped. Mr. Wang walked the rows checking points, and when he reached Emile he counted seven correct, then paused at one near the bottom left. "Which quadrant is this in?" Emile looked at the point, negative 3 and negative 6, sitting in the bottom left section. "Three," he said. Mr. Wang nodded and moved on.

Merrick kicked Emile's chair on his way to hand in his sheet. "Ten points. The homework pass is mine." Emile let his eyes drift back to his own grid, where the seven points had begun to line up into a straight path, one that climbed steadily toward quadrant one. He traced the line with his pencil, wondering where it had been before it crossed into quadrant two, up past where his paper ended.

activity: to draw a room in two-point perspective with two vanishing points
knowledge_domain: to draw a room in two-point perspective with two vanishing points
fact: Two-point perspective is used when you look at a corner, so each of the two walls meeting at that corner recedes toward its own vanishing point.
story:
The community art studio smelled like pencil shavings and wet paint, and Elijah loved it more than almost anywhere else. He had signed up to participate in the Saturday drawing workshop because the flyer promised "cities, castles, and impossible rooms," and today was the last day before the youth show, where one drawing from each student would hang on the studio's front wall for a whole month.

"Twenty minutes," Mr. Hughes called out, walking between the easels. "The frames for the show get hung at noon, sharp."

Elijah stared at his paper in despair. He had drawn a fantastic castle corridor with tall pillars and banners, the kind a dragon might guard, but every pillar leaned the wrong way, as if the whole hallway were melting. He had used one vanishing point at the center, the way he always did, and it worked fine when he drew a road running straight at you. It was ruining everything here.

Hafsa leaned over from the next easel, her own paper showing a cozy living room with a fireplace. "Your castle looks kind of venomous," she said. "Like it's going to bite somebody."

"It's not supposed to be venomous. It's supposed to be grand." Elijah pushed the drawing back and wandered to the window, where Katelyn was sketching the corner of the actual studio room, the corner where the brick wall met the plaster wall. Her lines ran off in two different directions, left and right, toward two little dots on the far edges of her paper.

"Why two dots?" he asked.

Katelyn shrugged. "Because I'm looking at the corner. Each wall goes back its own way, so each one runs toward its own dot."

Elijah felt something click, the way a jar lid does when it finally loosens. He was facing the corner of his castle corridor, not staring straight down it. The left wall needed one vanishing point and the right wall needed a different one. He hurried back to his easel, but his paper was smudged and crowded, and there was no time to erase everything.

"Fresh sheet," Mr. Hughes said gently, setting one down. "Ten minutes. The frames are an expense the studio only covers once a year, so we hang them on schedule."

Elijah placed two dots, one near each edge of the paper, and drew the corner pillar first, tall and proud. Then he let every pillar on the left wall lean toward the left dot and every pillar on the right wall lean toward the right dot. The corridor opened up in front of him like a mouth about to sing.

"Time," Mr. Hughes announced. "Bring your drawings to the front."

Elijah carried his castle forward, still warm from his hand. Hafsa looked at it and grinned.

"Still a little venomous," she said, "but in a good way."

activity: to mediate an argument between two friends without taking a side
knowledge_domain: to mediate an argument between two friends without taking a side
fact: In mediation, each person usually gets to tell their side without being interrupted while the other person listens.
story:
Ethan had exactly one hour before his grandmother's bees needed checking, and somehow Elise and Cory had turned her kitchen table into a battlefield. "He deleted the whole database," Elise said, jabbing a finger at Cory. "Three weeks of bee counts. Gone."

"I did not delete it," Cory shot back. "I was sorting it." They talked over each other, louder and louder, while Ethan's grandmother slid a plate of biscuits toward him and disappeared into the garden with a grin, like she knew something he didn't.

Ethan's plan had been simple: figure out who was right, shake the loser's hand, done. But they kept interrupting each other, and every interruption started a new argument about the interruption itself. He watched them go around twice more, and a thought landed like a dropped biscuit. The interruptions were the problem, not the accident. What if nobody got to talk over anybody? He held up both hands. "New rule. One at a time, no cutting in. Elise first, all the way to the end. Then Cory, all the way to the end. That's it."

"That's how mediation works?" Cory asked.

"That's how this one works," Ethan said, feeling oddly official.

Elise told her side without a single interruption, and halfway through, Cory's mouth opened and then closed again, because Ethan pointed at the chair like a traffic cop. When Cory finally got his turn, the story came out whole: he had clicked "sort" while the file was saving, and the records hadn't vanished, they had scattered into the wrong folders. He hadn't deleted anything. He had hidden it. Ten minutes of searching got every number back, and Elise actually laughed.

Out in the garden, the bees were droning over the squash blossoms, busy pollinating the last flowers of summer, and Ethan lifted a frame of comb toward the light. The new hive looked small and fragile, he thought, kind of vulnerable without its big sister colony beside it. He'd have to tell his grandmother they should double-wrap it before October.

"Same time next week?" Cory called from the porch. "Elise says she'll bring her notebook, and we promise to fight quietly."

"Bring cookies too," Ethan said. "Mediators need fuel."

activity: to understand the changes of puberty and why daily showers and deodorant matter
knowledge_domain: to understand the changes of puberty and why daily showers and deodorant matter
fact: During puberty the larynx, or voice box, grows larger and the vocal cords get longer and thicker, which makes the voice deeper, especially in boys.
story:
Lillian leaned against the picnic table outside the camp infirmary, reading the letter her mother had tucked into her duffel bag. "Your body is changing this year," her mom wrote, "and that means sweat glands that work harder, oilier hair, and a daily shower even when you're tired. Use the deodorant I packed. It's the purple stick, next to your toothbrush." Lillian sniffed her left armpit, then her right, and decided her mother had a point. She had skipped the shower after the morning hike, and her cabin, Cedar Cabin, smelled like wet socks.

After lunch, Mr. Kaya called the campers to the amphitheater for presentations. Each camper had to recount a nature observation from the week, and Lillian had written hers about the beaver dam by the north creek. She went third, and halfway through her description of the dam's climax, the moment the water finally rose over the top, a boy from Juniper Cabin stood up to present and his voice cracked so hard on his second sentence that a girl in the back row giggled.

He pushed on, but his voice dropped low, jumped high, and broke again on the word "osprey." He sat down red-faced, and Lillian heard two boys behind her whisper that he was faking it for laughs. She thought about her mom's letter. Bodies changing. She had noticed her own arms smelling different this summer, and Nathalie had shot up two inches and needed new sneakers in July. Maybe the boy's voice was changing too, and it wasn't something he could control.

At free swim, Lillian found Isabella, who had a worn and durable paperback about growing up that her older sister had given her. "Can I borrow it?" Lillian asked. "Trade you my second popsicle." Isabella handed it over, and Lillian sat on the dock with her feet in the water, the pages warm from the sun, smelling faintly of sunscreen. In the chapter on voices she found the answer: during puberty the larynx, or voice box, grows larger and the vocal cords get longer and thicker, which makes the voice deeper, especially in boys.

The next morning the boy from Juniper Cabin was called up again to finish his presentation. He stood stiff, braced for laughter. Before he started, Lillian raised her hand. "His larynx is growing," she said. "It's his voice box. The vocal cords get longer and thicker, and that makes the voice deeper." Mr. Kaya nodded and told the giggling girl in the back row to listen closely, because in a few years everyone's body would surprise them somehow.

The boy's voice still cracked on "osprey," but nobody laughed, and he grinned at Lillian on his way back to his seat. That night she lined up first for the shower, purple deodorant stick in hand.

activity: getting a first pair of glasses
knowledge_domain: getting a first pair of glasses
fact: In nearsightedness, light from distant objects focuses in front of the retina instead of on it, most often because the eyeball is slightly too long.
story:
Marcus had been squinting at the whiteboard from the back row for two weeks, and he had a theory about it. His eyes worked fine up close. He could read the tiny text on his dad's phone, count crumbs on the counter, see every detail on a trading card held six inches from his nose. It was only far things that went blurry, like the board, or the street sign at the end of the block. That seemed like a clue, and he wanted to test it before his eye appointment on Saturday.

"So you're saying near stuff is easy and far stuff is fuzzy," said Ali, who had come over to build the pond diorama for their science project. She was painting a lily pad while he talked. "That's the opposite of my grandpa. He holds the menu at arm's length."

"My theory," Marcus said, "is that my eyeballs are the wrong shape. Like, too long, front to back. So the light from far away lands in the wrong place, in front of the back of my eye instead of right on it." He drew a quick sketch in his notebook: a circle with an arrow stopping short of the back wall. "The picture forms too early. That's why it's fuzzy."

"Is that plausible?" Ali asked, squinting at the drawing. "Can an eyeball be too long?"

"That's what I'm going to find out. Want to help me test it?" He taped a page of small print to the fence at the bottom of the yard, then stood at the porch steps and tried to read it. He could make out the headline but not the rest. When he walked halfway down, the words sharpened. He wrote the results on a clipboard, feeling like a real scientist studying the ecosystem of his own backyard, which was a funny thought because normally the ecosystem project was the exciting one.

On Saturday, the optometrist flipped lenses in front of Marcus's face and asked which was better, one or two. Marcus confided his theory right there in the chair, the eyeball being too long, the light stopping in front of where it should land. The optometrist smiled. "Nearsighted," he said. "That's the word for it. You figured out most of it yourself."

When the glasses arrived a week later, Marcus put them on in the kitchen and ran straight to the back door. The fence at the bottom of the yard had letters on it, actual readable letters. He could see the small print from the porch. He could see everything.

"Ali!" he shouted into the phone. "I can read the fence!"

activity: to build a simple circuit with a battery, a switch and a bulb and explain why it lights
knowledge_domain: to build a simple circuit with a battery, a switch and a bulb and explain why it lights
fact: In a series circuit, if one bulb breaks, the loop is broken and every bulb in it goes out.
story:
Daniel had exactly twelve minutes to make his bulb light up, and so far the bulb was winning.

"It's not fair," said Jase, peering over the cluttered lab table. "Harlee's bulb glowed on the first try. Hers is obviously immune to failure."

"Nothing is immune to failure," Daniel said, wiggling the wire again. "My proof is this bulb." The battery sat there like a smug gray brick. The switch was flipped, the wires were clipped, and the bulb stayed dark. Mr. Tse had said the demo teams would be picked at two o'clock sharp, and the clock above the whiteboard read 1:48. If Daniel's circuit didn't work, he'd be the only kid in class presenting a table full of dead parts.

He stared at the loop. Battery, wire, switch, bulb, wire, back to battery. It looked exactly like the diagram on the board. "Maybe the battery's dead," he said, and swapped it for a fresh one from the supply drawer. Nothing. "Maybe the bulb's loose." He screwed it tighter. Still nothing.

Then Harlee wandered over, holding her glowing circuit like a trophy. "Try her bulb in yours," Jase suggested. Daniel unplugged his bulb and clipped Harlee's into his loop instead. It lit instantly. "So it's the bulb," Daniel said, feeling both relieved and annoyed. He grabbed a new bulb from the drawer, clipped it in, and the loop glowed warm and yellow. He flipped the switch off and on twice, just to enjoy the power.

"Okay, but why does it work at all?" Harlee asked, tapping his battery. "The electricity's invisible. How do you know it goes around?"

"Because it's a loop," Daniel said. "It has to travel all the way around, through everything, and back. If the loop gets broken anywhere, nothing flows at all." He pulled the dead bulb out of his pocket and held it up. "Watch." He clipped the old dead bulb back into the circuit alongside the good one, so the current had to pass through both. Both bulbs went dark. Even the good one. "See? One dead bulb kills the whole string, because the loop is broken."

"That's kind of dramatic," said Jase.

"That's science," said Daniel, removing the dead bulb. The good one lit again instantly, and he grinned like he'd invented fire.

Mr. Tse checked the clock and clapped his hands. "Two o'clock. Demo teams, to your stations."

Daniel flipped his switch one last time. "Go on, little loop," he whispered. "Make the trip."

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: The parable of the blind men and the elephant, from ancient India, describes people who each touch a different part of an elephant and describe it completely differently.
story:
Lucy pushed through the door of the science room with her backpack still on one shoulder, and she knew immediately that something was wrong. Delia and Kohen were standing on opposite sides of the workbench, arms crossed, and the invention they were supposed to finish by Friday sat between them like a dropped cake.

"It's a grabber arm," Delia insisted. "I saw Mr. Bélanger's sketch. It has claws and a hinge, and it picks things up."

"It's obviously a launcher," Kohen said. "I was here Tuesday when he tested the base. It flings stuff. I watched a wooden ball hit the ceiling tile."

Lucy tilted her head. Both of them sounded certain, and both of them sounded right, which was strange. How could one machine be two things? She leaned over the workbench and studied the half-built contraption, noticing that the claw end and the spring-loaded base didn't actually touch each other yet. Nobody in the club had seen the whole thing at once, she realized. Delia had come Thursday, Kohen Tuesday, and Lucy herself had only read the supply list. They were each describing a different part.

"It's like that story my grandma tells," Delia said, her arms slowly uncrossing. "The blind men and the elephant. It's a parable from ancient India. One touches the trunk and says it's a snake, one touches a leg and says it's a tree, and each one swears the others are gullible fools who can't feel the truth right in front of them."

"That's us," Lucy said, and she had to press her lips together to keep from laughing. "We've each got one part and we've built a whole different elephant in our heads." The idea provoked her into motion more than the argument ever had. If the parts were real, then the machine was real, and the only thing missing was somebody willing to connect them.

She picked up the piston from the parts tray, the metal cylinder Mr. Bélanger had left beside a diagram neither of them had noticed, and held it up between the claw and the base. "So what if the launcher throws it, and the claw catches it? A catch-and-throw machine."

Kohen picked up the diagram and unfolded it all the way, and Delia reached for the screwdriver.

"Team elephant," Delia said, and Lucy fitted the piston into place.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: Grief can affect the body as well as feelings, often causing tiredness, trouble sleeping or changes in appetite.
story:
Charlotte stood at the kitchen counter on Thursday morning, staring at the bowl of cereal she had poured and then not touched, just like Tuesday's toast and Wednesday's eggs. She had slept maybe three hours last night, and the night before that, and her legs felt like they were full of wet sand. She pressed the back of her hand to her forehead the way Grandma used to do, checking for fever, because in her head she was building a case: no appetite, no sleep, no energy. Those were symptoms. She was getting sick, exactly one week after the funeral, and she could not get sick before the science test on Friday.

She found the thermometer in the drawer by the stove and sat on the floor to wait for the beep. Dereck knocked on the back door, saw her sitting there, and let himself in. "Are you contagious?" he asked, keeping a careful distance. "I came for the flashcards." Charlotte held up the thermometer. Ninety-eight point two. Normal. "Then why do I feel like a collapsed tent?" she said.

Mr. Ong, the neighbour from across the fence, came by at lunch with a container of soup, because that was the kind of neighbour he was, and he had known Grandma for thirty years. Charlotte told him her evidence, laying it out piece by piece like a lab report. He set the soup down and nodded slowly. "When my father died, I couldn't eat for days, and I'd lie awake till two in the morning," he said. "The doctor told me grief doesn't only live in the feelings. It can affect the body too. Tiredness, trouble sleeping, changes in appetite." Charlotte looked at the thermometer still in her hand. "So I'm not sick," she said. "I'm just grieving all the way through." Mr. Ong said that sounded about right.

She tried an experiment. She ate four spoonfuls of the soup, which was more than she had managed in three days, and then went out back and did a vigorous ten minutes of shooting baskets with Dereck, hoping her body would finally feel tired enough to sleep. That night she lay in bed listening to the house creak, and for once she did not fight it. She thought of Grandma pressing the back of her cool hand to Charlotte's forehead, checking, always checking, and she budgeted herself one memory before letting her eyes close. "Night, Grandma," she whispered into the dark, and pulled the blanket up to her chin.

activity: to sort rocks as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic by how they were formed
knowledge_domain: to sort rocks as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic by how they were formed
fact: Sedimentary rock forms when layers of sediment such as sand, mud or shells are pressed together and cemented over time.
story:
Alexander pressed his nose almost to the glass case, staring at a slice of rock the color of stale bread. Thin dark stripes ran across it, one after another, like the growth rings on the tree stump in his grandmother's yard.

"Why does rock have layers?" he asked. "Rocks aren't trees."

Gurfateh leaned in beside him. "Maybe it's painted?" He tapped the case, and a museum attendant gave them a look that made him step back fast.

The planetarium's side hall held a geology exhibit, and Mr. Müller had given them a sorting task: twelve rocks on a felt tray, three labeled boxes, igneous, sedimentary, metamorphic. Alexander had already put the speckled black one in igneous, since it looked frozen, like something that had cooled from a melt. The striped one was the problem.

Kadence slid her tray next to his. "I'm stuck on that one too," she said. She turned hers over, and the back showed the same stripes, faint shell shapes pressed between the bands. Alexander grabbed his magnifying loupe and looked again. Shells. And in the next stripe, grains like beach sand, then something like dried mud.

"Think about it backwards," he said slowly. "Sand settles on a river bottom. Mud settles on top of the sand. Shells settle on top of the mud. If the layers get pressed together and stuck over time..." He trailed off, turning the rock in his hand. "That's what this is. Layers. Sandwich rock."

"Sedimentary," Kadence read off the box label, and laughed. "Okay, that actually fits."

They tested the idea on the rest of the tray. Anything striped or grainy or full of fossils went into sedimentary. When Mr. Müller came by, he raised an eyebrow at their full box.

"You three want to accommodate the rest of us and share the reasoning?" he asked.

"Layers mean it piled up," Alexander said. "Sand, mud, shells, pressed together over time. We checked every rock for stripes."

Mr. Müller's grin was contagious. "Well then. From that perspective, the whole cliff outside is a history book."

Alexander looked back at the striped slice, at the little shells trapped between the bands. "Then this one read like a beach," he said.

activity: to write a five-paragraph persuasive essay with an introduction and a conclusion
knowledge_domain: to write a five-paragraph persuasive essay with an introduction and a conclusion
fact: A persuasive essay is stronger when it states the best opposing argument fairly and then answers it; this answer is called a rebuttal.
story:
George had to write a five-paragraph persuasive essay by Monday, and he had chosen to argue that the school library needed more money for new books. He spread his draft across the kitchen table at his grandpa's house, where he went every Saturday, and glared at it. The introduction was fine. The three middle paragraphs were fine. The conclusion was one sentence long, and he had a feeling Ms. Friedman would not call that fine.

His friend Ariyah was coming over to work on her own essay, and when she arrived she dropped her backpack on a chair and read over his shoulder. "You only wrote your side," she said.

"That's the point. It's persuasive."

"Mine's about longer lunch. I wrote a whole paragraph saying twenty minutes is short but it saves class time, and then I answered it. My cousin told me that's the strongest part." She tapped his page. "It's called a rebuttal."

George didn't believe her. If he said the other side had a point, wouldn't that wreck his argument? He decided to test it. He wrote a fourth paragraph, which meant rearranging everything: he moved one of his book paragraphs into the introduction, put the new paragraph third, and kept two for his side. In it he admitted that the school had to spread its money across sports gear, field trips and repairs. Then he answered it: the library was the only place some kids got books at all, and its shelves held titles older than their parents.

He read both versions aloud to his grandpa, who was peeling potatoes at the counter. "The second one," his grandpa said. "I wanted to argue with the first one. The second one, you already argued with me."

On Sunday, George evaluated the draft one last time, cutting a sentence he'd liked about his resentment toward the budget committee, since it sounded more like a grudge than a reason. He kept the sentence about kids standing in line for the four books worth reading in an impoverished collection.

On Monday, Ms. Friedman handed the essays back. At the top of his page she had written one word and circled it: "Rebuttal. Nice." George folded the paper along the crease and slid it into his binder, keeping it where he could find it again.

activity: to write a Python loop that prints the times table for any number the user types
knowledge_domain: to write a Python loop that prints the times table for any number the user types
fact: A Python f-string such as f"{n} x {i} = {n * i}" places the values of variables and calculations directly into the printed text.
story:
Madison wanted her times table program to look like the ones printed on the back of her math notebook, neat rows reading "7 x 1 = 7," but every time she ran it, the screen showed a jumble of curly braces and letters instead of numbers. The clock on the wall of the computer lab said coding club had twenty minutes left, and she had already erased her code twice.

"Mine just prints n times i equals something," said Seerat, leaning over from the next seat. "Ms. Chea says that's close, but it looks like the computer is muttering to itself."

"I want mine to look real," Madison said. "Like a table a teacher would hang on the wall." She had the loop working; she knew it would count from one to ten. The rebellious part was the printing, where her words came out wrong no matter how carefully she typed them.

Halle slid her chair over, holding her own laptop like a tray of cookies she was sharing. "Watch this," she said, and typed a small f before the quotation marks in her print line. On her screen appeared "6 x 4 = 24," each number sitting exactly where it belonged. Madison stared at it. The f had to be the hidden cause, the small thing making all the difference, invisible in the output but doing the work.

She tried it on her own line. She typed the letter f, kept the quotation marks, and put her variables and the multiplication inside the braces. When she ran the program, her heart did a small hop. There it was, row after row: "7 x 1 = 7," "7 x 2 = 14," all the way to "7 x 10 = 70," with the answers calculated and placed right into the text.

"Madison, look at yours!" Seerat said. "It's the real thing." She had been stuck trying to build her lines with commas and plus signs, and every attempt seemed to evade her, sliding into an error message the moment she ran it.

"Type a small f before the quotes," Madison said. "Then whatever's inside the braces turns into its value." She pointed at her own screen so Seerat could see the braces holding n times i. "You don't have to glue the pieces together with plus signs."

Seerat typed it, ran it, and her screen filled with clean rows too. She grinned so wide that Ms. Chea came over to see what the two of them were laughing about. The teacher read their tables top to bottom, then quietly added a sticky note to Madison's laptop that said, "Show the club next week." Madison put the note in her pocket, where it would not bend or fracture, and started changing her seven to a twelve.

activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
knowledge_domain: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
fact: As a broken bone heals, the body forms a callus, a mass of cartilage and new bone that bridges the gap between the broken ends.
story:
Addison sat on the bleachers at the edge of the soccer field, her left arm resting in a sling, watching Lyana take her spot at center midfield. Four weeks ago, that spot had been hers. She could still trace the whole play in her mind: the abrupt lunge for the ball, the wet grass, her wrist folding under her at exactly the wrong angle. Sometimes she wondered if she should have just let the ball go out of bounds. Coach had never said so, but the look on her face that day had been loud enough.

"Earth to Addison," Nadia said, dropping onto the bench beside her with a water bottle. "You're staring at the field like it insulted you."

"It kind of did." Addison tapped her cast with two fingers. "I have a follow-up appointment tomorrow. Another X-ray."

"Are you hoping it's healed or not healed?" Nadia asked. "Because last week you said if it wasn't healed, you didn't have to decide whether to try out for club team, and that would be easier."

"I didn't say easier. I said less complicated." Addison frowned. "There's a difference."

At the appointment the next afternoon, the doctor slid the new X-ray up onto the light board next to the old one. Addison leaned forward. On the first image, the bone ended in two clean, separate lines. On the new one, right between those lines, was a fuzzy gray lump, like a small cloud parked where the break used to be.

"What is that?" she asked.

"That's the callus," the doctor said. "It means the bone is healing. It's a mass of cartilage and new bone that bridges the gap between the broken ends." She tapped the cloud with the cap of her pen. "It has to be there before the bone gets strong again."

Addison studied the two X-rays, going back and forth. So the fuzziness was the healing itself. She had been thinking of healing as something invisible, a quiet thing happening in the dark, but here it was, drawn on film. She thought of her grandmother's wrist last year, which the family had argued about endlessly, a small controversy over whether she'd really needed the surgery. Nobody had ever mentioned a callus. Maybe if they'd seen one, they would have stopped arguing.

"Can I have a copy?" she asked.

At Saturday's practice, she found Lyana and Nadia by the goal net and held up the printout. "See this lump? That's my bone rebuilding itself. It's actually doing something in there."

"So you're coming back," Lyana said. It wasn't quite a question.

"I'm coming back." Addison had made the decision somewhere between the light board and the field, though she couldn't point to the exact moment. She looked at the X-ray one more time, folded it carefully, and tucked it into her pocket where she could feel the paper's edge against her hip.

"Then you'd better start running," Nadia said, nodding toward the far goal, where the rest of the team was already lined up.

Addison got up off the bleachers and jogged out onto the grass.

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: A boundary is a limit a person sets about what they are comfortable with, such as how others treat them, touch them or use their belongings.
story:
Andrew pushed his pasta around the plate while his dad talked about the neighbor's fence, and all he could think about was the empty seat where his phone should have been. Confiscated until Friday. Confiscated because of what he had done with it at lunch, and that was the part he kept turning over like a stone in his pocket.

He remembered it clearly. Lilian had left her phone on the lunch table while she went back through the line for a second roll, and Cayson had nudged it toward Andrew and said, "Her messages are probably hilarious." Andrew had picked it up and read the first three texts on the screen, which were not hilarious at all. They were from her mom, about her grandmother being sick, and about how Lilian's anxiety had been bad all week. Then Lilian was standing there, her face gone tight, saying, "Put it down. You don't read my phone without asking. Ever." She had said the word for it, too, the word Mr. Korhonen's health poster used: "That's a boundary. It means what I'm comfortable with, like how people treat me, touch me, or use my stuff."

At dinner, his dad mentioned carbohydrates in the sauce, some joke about marathon training, and Andrew said "yeah" without hearing it. He was working on a theory. He had thought Lilian was angry because he had seen something embarrassing, but embarrassing things had never bothered her before. She had once laughed for ten minutes about her own bad haircut photo. The pattern didn't fit. He drafted a different explanation in his head, the way he drafted an essay, sentence by sentence: she was under stress already, her grandmother was sick, and the phone was one thing in her life she had control over. When he picked it up, he took even that away. He hadn't crossed a line he could see. He had crossed one only she could see, because it was hers.

That, he decided, was testable. His idea was simple: the apology was not about the texts themselves, it was about the taking without asking. If he apologized for reading, and offered something back, some control, the theory would hold.

He ate fast, cleared his plate, and asked to borrow the family tablet. His dad handed it over, still talking about fences. Andrew wrote three drafts before anything came out coherent, then crossed out the version that explained himself, because explaining was for his benefit, not hers. The final message was two sentences: "I was wrong to read your phone without asking. From now on I won't touch it, or anything of yours, unless you say it's okay." He would hand it to her in person tomorrow, at the table by the window, and wait for whatever she decided.

He set the tablet down on the kitchen counter, screen still glowing.

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In Chinese culture, a clock is usually avoided as a gift, because the phrase 'giving a clock' sounds like a phrase about attending someone's death.
story:
The fortune cookie sat untouched on Liam's plate while he stared at the glass case by the register, where a small brass clock ticked away between a teapot and a jade dragon. He had twenty minutes before Ivy's family arrived at the Golden Palace to celebrate their new house, and he still had no gift.

"I still think the clock was perfect," said Marlee, dunking a spring roll in sauce. "Twelve dollars. Cute little sailboat hands. Done."

"Ivy said her grandmother would be upset, but she wouldn't say why." Liam lowered his voice. "She just grabbed my arm in the mall and said, 'Not the clock, not the clock,' like it was a snake."

"Maybe her grandmother hates clocks."

"That doesn't make sense. She has a clock in her kitchen. Ivy told me." Liam broke the cookie in half and ignored the fortune slip. He was trying to work out the pattern. Ivy's family had accepted the teapot Marlee's mom gave them last year with no problem. They had accepted Marlee's drawing of their old apartment. Why would a clock be different? It had to be about the gift itself, not the object, and gifts meant something. Maybe the clock meant something in Chinese.

He stood up so fast he knocked his chopsticks off the table.

"Where are you going?"

"To ask the cashier." The cashier, an older man with reading glasses pushed up on his forehead, was wrapping a to-go order. Liam leaned on the counter. "Excuse me. If I gave a clock as a gift to a Chinese family, would that be bad?"

The cashier stopped folding the box and looked at Liam over his glasses. "A clock? No, no. In Chinese, giving a clock sounds like attending someone's death. Very unlucky."

"Oh no. I almost did that."

"Then you are smart boy," the cashier said, and gave him a wrapped tangerine from the counter. "For the new house. Tangerine is lucky."

Liam carried it back to the table like it was made of glass. Marlee squinted at it. "A tangerine? That's your whole gift?"

"It's lucky, and it doesn't sound like anything terrible."

When Ivy's family came in, her grandmother took the tangerine in both hands, smiled wide, and said something to Ivy in Cantonese. Ivy translated, grinning: "She says you're too clever to be spending your pension on fruit."

"I don't have a pension," Liam said. "I have fifty dollars of birthday money, and I spent twelve of it on a clock I can't give anybody."

"Then it's your clock now," said Marlee. "Perfect for timing how long it takes your face to turn red."

Liam slid the fortune slip across the table to her. It read: You will avoid one great mistake today.

activity: to sing in two-part harmony with a choir and hold their part against the other
knowledge_domain: to sing in two-part harmony with a choir and hold their part against the other
fact: In staggered breathing, choir members take breaths at different moments, so a long note keeps sounding even though every singer breathes.
story:
Nicholas stood in the choir loft of St. Brigid's with the sheet music shaking slightly in his hands. Mr. Oliveira had prescribed the exact order of the rehearsal: warm-ups first, then the lower voices alone, then the two parts together. Nicholas sang the lower line, and every time the upper voices came in, his part slid upward to chase theirs, like a dog after a thrown ball. It was embarrassing. He was twelve, and Abygael, who was eleven and had joined the choir three weeks after him, held her line without wobbling at all.

He remembered his grandfather at the kitchen table last summer, sorting coins from a jar. "Trust is a currency," the old man had said, sliding a worn dime across the wood. "You spend it whether you mean to or not." Nicholas had shrugged then, but tonight the words came back to him. He had spent something too, telling Mr. Oliveira he could handle a harmony part when he had never once sung against another line. Maybe he should have admitted it. He stared at the page and wondered whether to raise his hand.

Instead, he tried an experiment. The final note of the anthem was long, longer than one breath could hold, and he had noticed something odd at the last rehearsal: the note never stopped, even though he could hear singers breathing. He had been listening for the sound of the note when he should have been listening for the silences inside it. They came at different moments, one singer slipping out to breathe while the others carried on, and none of them lined up. When Nehemiah, standing beside him, took a breath halfway through the note, Abygael's voice simply filled the space. Nicholas realized the long note was not one person's job. It belonged to everyone, passed along like a bucket in a line.

"It's called staggered breathing," Nehemiah whispered, when Nicholas mentioned it during the break. "Mr. Oliveira says we all breathe at different times so the note keeps sounding."

They ran the anthem again. When the upper voices entered, Nicholas stopped chasing them. He thought of the note as a rope stretched between the two sections, and he held his end while Abygael held hers. On the final note, he waited, watched Nehemiah breathe, then took his own breath in the gap that followed. The sound above him stayed lush and unbroken, and his low line ran beneath it like a river under ice.

Afterward, Mr. Oliveira raised one eyebrow. "That held," he said.

Nicholas grinned and tucked the music into his folder. "Next time give me the harder part."

activity: going to a first sleepover at a friend's house
knowledge_domain: going to a first sleepover at a friend's house
fact: A scary story can set off a real fear response, with a racing heart and faster breathing, even when the listener knows it is made up.
story:
Levi had never been to a sleepover before, and he had decided to presume it would go fine, the way he presumed the school bus would come: probably, until it didn't. Now he was in Sabrina's basement rec room with two sleeping bags, a bowl of popcorn, and a lamp shaped like a football. Adelle had come too, because Sabrina's mom said three was a good number for a first time.

At ten o'clock Sabrina turned off the lamp. In the dark she told a story about a previous owner of the house who had fallen down these very basement stairs and now climbed them again on the anniversary of that night, one slow step at a time, dragging something behind her. Sabrina made the dragging sound with her sneaker against the carpet. Levi knew the story was made up, because Sabrina had got it from a video and had told him so herself the day before. Still, his heart started thumping hard, and his breathing went quick and shallow, so quick that Adelle whispered, "Are you okay?"

"Testing something," Levi whispered back. He found his own pulse on his wrist and counted. Fast. He breathed in slowly through his nose, the way he did before a spelling test, and told himself, out loud but quietly, "It's a story. It is one hundred percent made up." His heart did not slow down. That interested him. His brain knew the fact, but his body was acting like the fact wasn't true, and the two things were happening at the same time, in the same organism, which was him.

Then something creaked on the stairs. One slow step.

Levi sat straight up. His heart was now going so fast he could feel it in his ears. The creak came again, closer, and Adelle grabbed his sleeve, and Sabrina, who had been telling the story in a low voice, went completely silent. Levi stared at the rectangle of the doorway, where the dark was a slightly different dark.

A cat walked in. It was orange, fat, and defiant about being locked out, and it crossed the rec room, stepped onto Sabrina's sleeping bag, and lay down on her feet as if nothing had happened. Sabrina's laugh came out in one loud burst. "That's just Biscuit! He always comes down here."

"Even knowing it was fake," Levi said, still holding his own wrist, "my heart's still going like I ran the block."

"Same," said Adelle. "Same exact thing." Biscuit purred on Sabrina's feet, and the three of them lay listening to it in the dark.

activity: trying out for a school sports team
knowledge_domain: trying out for a school sports team
fact: Many school pools are 25 yards or 25 meters long, called short course, while Olympic swimming races are held in 50-meter pools, called long course.
story:
Tyler laced his shoes so tight his fingers ached, because today was the day, track tryouts, and he had been waiting all winter for this. Ms. Barrett blew her whistle from the infield of the running track and called the first heat of the mile to the line. Tyler bounced on his toes. His problem was simple and huge: the team roster restricted the squad to twelve runners, and thirteen kids were trying out. Somebody was going to get cut, and he refused to be that somebody.

He ran with his head up, watching the runners ahead of him, and finished fourth, which felt like flying. While he caught his breath on the grass, his friend Hana came stomping across the infield, waving her phone. "I didn't make swim team," she said. "Coach said my tryout time wasn't fast enough. Thirty-two seconds for my fifty free. I used to go twenty-nine!" She shoved the phone at him. On the screen was an old result, a race from a summer invitational, twenty-nine point one seconds.

Tyler squinted at it. Something didn't line up, and he wanted to fix it more than he wanted his own time. "Where was that meet?" he asked. "Some big aquatic center. Huge pool." Tyler remembered his cousin complaining about the same thing last summer. "Wait. Was that an Olympic-size pool? Fifty meters all the way across?" Hana shrugged. "Fifty meters, yeah. Our school pool is twenty-five."

"That's it," Tyler said, already grinning. "Lots of school pools are twenty-five yards or twenty-five meters, called short course. The long ones, fifty meters, are called long course. Your old time is from a long course pool. You can't compare it straight across with your tryout." Hana stared at him. "So I'm not actually slower?" "You're not actually slower," Tyler said. "You need to prove it, though."

Hana looked at the track, then at the pool building beyond the fence. "Coach is still in the pool office. Come on." They ran the whole way, Tyler still in his spikes, clacking across the pavement like a happy woodpecker. In the office, Hana laid her phone on the desk, pointed at the meet results, and asked for one more trial swim. The coach frowned, tapped the screen, looked at the pool, and pulled a stopwatch out of the drawer. "Lane three," he said. "Suit up."

Tyler leaned on the doorframe of the natatorium as Hana climbed onto the blocks, and he cupped his hands around his mouth. "Go!"

activity: to build a simple circuit with a battery, a switch and a bulb and explain why it lights
knowledge_domain: to build a simple circuit with a battery, a switch and a bulb and explain why it lights
fact: Bulb filaments are made of tungsten because it has the highest melting point of any pure metal, about 3,400 degrees Celsius.
story:
Georgia crouched on the concrete floor of her garage, staring at a battery, a switch, three wires, and a stubborn little bulb that refused to light. Tomorrow she had to stand up in class and explain why a bulb lights when you close a switch, and Lily-Anne had already promised to film it. One more humiliation in front of the whole class was not on Georgia's list of plans.

Last Saturday at the science museum, she and Eason had pressed their faces against a magnifier that showed a glowing thread inside a spare bulb. "It's tungsten," Eason had read off the display. "Filaments are made of tungsten because it has the highest melting point of any pure metal, about 3,400 degrees Celsius." Eason wanted to film a video about it for the school news channel, and he kept saying Georgia's demo would be the perfect ending. She had agreed before she could actually make the thing work.

She checked the wires again. The battery end felt right, the switch clicked, but the bulb sat dark. Maybe the bulb itself was dead, she thought. Maybe the wire had a break hidden under the plastic. She couldn't see electricity, so she had to guess at the invisible path it took. Then she had an idea. She unscrewed the bulb and touched the two wires directly together for half a second. A tiny spark snapped. The wires, the battery, the switch: all fine. The problem was hiding inside the bulb.

She dug through the coffee can of parts and found another bulb, screwed it in, and flipped the switch. Light bloomed, warm and yellow across the dusty workbench. Georgia sat very still, watching it, imagining that thread of tungsten heating until it glowed without melting, hotter than anything in her kitchen, surviving 3,400 degrees Celsius because no other pure metal could.

Eason came through the side door with his camera already raised, and she heard the little red light blink on. "Wait," Georgia said, holding up one finger. "First I have to mimic the museum display. Zoom in close." She cupped the bulb so the filament showed, thin and bright as a hair of fire, and said, "Rolling."

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: Slow breathing with long exhales can calm the body's stress response, which is why it is a common coping skill before a stressful moment.
story:
Chase sat on the end of his bed with his goalie glove on his knee, staring at the sixty-one text messages in the hockey team group chat. Tomorrow was tryouts, and the coach would run penalty shots at the end, one shooter against one goalie, everyone watching. His heart picked up speed just thinking about it, and his hands had gone cold and damp in a way he recognized. Last spring, before the exam, he had felt exactly like this, and his mother had said the word anxiety out loud like it was a weather report. He hated that feeling, but tonight he wanted to know whether he could do something about it.

He called Conrad, who was sprawled on his own bed three streets away, face lit blue by his screen. "Do you get all shaky before penalty shots?" Chase asked. "Not shaky," Conrad said. "More like my brain plays a horror movie starring me." Chase nodded at the screen. "My mom says that's stress. The body doing too much at once." He told Conrad about the older goalie at summer camp, the one who never looked rattled. Before every shot, that goalie had done the same strange thing: a long slow breath out, longer than the breath in, like he was letting air out of a valve one turn at a time. He'd called it his coping skill, something you practice before a stressful moment. "He said the long exhales calm your body down," Chase said. "I want to test it."

Conrad rolled his eyes, but he stayed on the call. "Test it how? You want me to shoot socks at you through the phone?" "Kind of," Chase said. He balled up three socks and set them on the dresser. He pictured each one as tomorrow's puck, imagined the shooter skating in, the whole gym holding its breath. First try, he breathed the way he normally did, quick and shallow, and his chest stayed tight, his glove hand slow. Then he tried the camp goalie's trick: slow inhale, then a long, long exhale, counting it out, letting the tightness leak away like pressure through a valve. Third sock, fourth sock, fifth. His hands warmed up. His glove moved where he wanted it to go. The tightness didn't vanish completely, but it dropped from a shout to a murmur, and that seemed to correspond directly to how steady he felt.

"Did it work?" Conrad asked. "I think so," Chase said. "I have to actually feel it to know. Tomorrow counts for real." He hung up, set his alarm, and put the glove beside his pillow where he'd see it first thing. Then he practiced once more, sitting cross-legged in the dark, long exhale after long exhale, until the sound of his own breathing was the only sound in the room. "Okay," he whispered to the glove. "Tomorrow we're the competent one."

activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
knowledge_domain: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
fact: Spanish adjectives usually come after the noun they describe, so "a black cat" is "un gato negro."
story:
Emma sat at the kitchen table with her notebook open to a page titled "Mi familia." Tomorrow she had to stand up in Ms. Bélanger's class and describe her family and her dog in Spanish, using full sentences, and so far all she had were scattered words. Her dog, Biscuit, lay under the table with one diagonal stripe of sunlight across his back, snoring. Emma wrote "Tengo un perro negro" and stared at it, because something about it felt wrong.

She had looked up "black dog" on her tablet earlier, and the translation had popped up as "perro negro." At the time she had shrugged and typed it into her notes, assuming the website had made some kind of mistake, or maybe swapped the words by accident. Websites did that. But now, testing the sentence out loud, she kept tripping over it. "I have a dog black," her brain insisted, and she frowned at the page. Her mother was out, and there was nobody to ask, so Emma decided to test it herself.

She typed "white cat" into the tablet. "Gato blanco." She typed "small house." "Casa pequeña." She sat back, pulse ticking a little faster, because a pattern was emerging and it was the same every single time. It wasn't a mistake. The website hadn't swapped anything. She wrote the words in a column, dog before black, cat before white, house before small, and tapped her pencil against the table. Spanish put the describing word second, after the thing it described. The whole concept flipped from what she was used to, and once she saw it, she couldn't unsee it.

Her phone buzzed. It was Leane, from Spanish class, and her message made Emma's stomach drop: "Did you finish your sentences? Mine sound so weird. I wrote tengo un gato negro and I think I did it wrong." Leane had translated her own cat's description the same backwards way Emma first had, and if Emma answered wrong, she could provoke a small disaster, because Leane would memorize whatever Emma said and repeat it in front of everyone tomorrow.

Emma typed back carefully. "You wrote it right. Un gato negro, that's how Spanish says it, black comes after cat. So a black cat is un gato negro." She reread it twice before sending, then tried one more test on the tablet, "big dog," and watched "perro grande" appear. Yes. Confident now, she crossed out nothing in her notebook, because it had all been right the first time. She practiced out loud, "Tengo un hermano menor. Tengo un perro negro," while Biscuit thumped his tail against the chair leg. Emma leaned down and told him, "Eres un perro negro," and he licked her hand.

activity: to read contour lines on a topographic map to find the steepest slope of a hill
knowledge_domain: to read contour lines on a topographic map to find the steepest slope of a hill
fact: The contour interval is the difference in height between one contour line and the next, and it is printed in the map's legend.
story:
Sydney spread the topographic map on a flat rock and pinned the corners with pinecones before the wind could steal it. "The bus leaves the trailhead at four thirty," Yousef said, checking his watch for the third time. "That gives us one hour to find the steepest slope, and I still want to set up my camera before dark. Owls are nocturnal, so they start hunting at dusk, and I need a good spot to film them."

Sydney traced the brown contour lines with her finger. Where the lines bunched tightly together, the hill dropped fast; where they spread apart, the ground was gentle. She counted the lines from the creek to the top of Hill 421. "Ten lines," she announced. "If each line is fifty feet, that's a five-hundred-foot climb."

Yousef frowned at the map. "The hill is only forty meters tall. I looked it up."

"That can't be right." Sydney counted again, then flipped the map over, searching. In the corner, in print so small she almost missed it, the legend said: contour interval 20 feet. "There. The contour interval is the difference in height between one contour line and the next, and it's printed right here in the legend. So it's only two hundred feet, not five hundred. I had it all wrong."

"Then the steep part isn't where you thought?"

Sydney leaned closer. The west face of Hill 421 had lines squeezed together like a dropped stack of pancakes. "No, look, it's still the west face. But shorter than I said, which means we can climb it and get down before the bus." She had to prioritize the steep slope over the easier eastern trail, since the whole point was to see it up close.

They scrambled up the western slope, boots slipping on loose shale, and at the top a drone buzzed past, its propellers whirring as it hovered over the trees below. Yousef lifted his camera and grinned. "Perfect angle for the owls."

Sydney folded the map along its worn crease and said, "Tomorrow, the tiny print in the legend gets read first."

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: Since 1996 the Internet Archive has been saving copies of public web pages, and its Wayback Machine lets anyone look at old versions of many websites.
story:
At dinner Matthew kept his phone face down beside his plate, which was against the rules, and everyone knew it meant something had happened.

"Zaid sent me a picture today," he said finally. "A screenshot of a web page. My web page. The one I made in third grade and deleted two years ago." His mother set down her fork. "Deleted things don't come back," she said. Matthew turned the phone over and slid it across the table. There was the blog, the ugly green banner, the post about his birthday party, exactly as he had left it. Under the post sat a photo of his dog on the front steps, and behind the dog, plain as anything, the house number. "Zaid says since 1996 something called the Internet Archive has been saving copies of public web pages," Matthew said. "He says there's a part of it, the Wayback Machine, that lets anyone look at old versions of websites. Anyone. Strangers." His father leaned closer to the screen, and nobody said anything for a moment.

Matthew explained what he had done that afternoon, because his mother asked him to clarify what he meant by deleted. He had gone to the archive himself and typed in the old address. He had expected an error. Instead a calendar appeared, dotted with dates, and when he clicked one, the whole page rebuilt itself in front of him, like a picture being un-erased. He had scrolled through every post, counting what a stranger could learn: his first name, his school's name from a spelling bee photo, the house number, and one post that said the family would be at the lake all weekend. A stranger could have read that and known the house was empty. That part he had not told Zaid.

"So the page is gone now?" his mother asked. "The real one, I mean." Matthew nodded. The real one was gone, and the copy was still sitting in the archive, patient and robust, the way a filing cabinet is robust, holding his third-grade self where anyone could find him. "Ms. Otieno says nothing you post really disappears," he said. "I thought she was just trying to scare us." His father looked at the photo of the dog for a long time. Then he pushed the phone gently back across the table. "Show me the calendar," he said.

activity: to create a strong password and explain why the same one should not be reused
knowledge_domain: to create a strong password and explain why the same one should not be reused
fact: NIST's guidance says systems should not force people to change passwords on a schedule, only when there is evidence a password has been stolen.
story:
Lily's mom had declared it Bring Your Daughter to Work Day, even though it wasn't, and Lily had already been given a lanyard, a desk, and one very important mission: set up her guest computer account. On the screen, a red banner glowed. "Your password has expired. Please choose a new one." That seemed strange, since she had never made one in the first place.

"New one every month," said the woman at the next desk, tapping her own keyboard. "That's the rule. The system makes us all comply, whether we like it or not." Lily typed "Sparky123" after her dog, but it refused it. She tried "SparkyJanuary" and then, feeling pessimistic about the whole enterprise, "SparkyJanuaryUgh." The system thought about that last one for a long moment and accepted it. Lily felt zero triumph.

At lunch, her mom's coworker from the polymer lab, Ms. Lewandowski, dropped into the chair beside them with a sandwich. Lily told her about the banner, mostly to complain. "Every month, a brand new password," she said. "By December I'll be on SparkyDecemberWhyDoIHateMyself."

Ms. Lewandowski laughed so hard she had to set the sandwich down. "Funny thing," she said. "The government standards people, NIST, actually say systems should not force people to change passwords on a schedule. Only when there's evidence a password has been stolen. But our system is old, and nobody wants to pay to fix it." She took another bite. "So we all pick SparkyFebruary and SparkyMarch and get a little less safe every month."

That afternoon, Lily thought about it while she was supposed to be practicing spreadsheet formulas. She had never seen anyone steal a password, but she could picture the pattern anyway: if everyone at the office added the month's name to the same old word, then anyone who saw one password could guess all the future ones. It was like hiding a key under the mat and then, for safety, moving it to under the flowerpot, the birdbath, and the gutter, and telling everyone you were clever. She decided to test it. She typed "momSparkyJanuary" into a notepad, then "momSparkyFebruary," and slid the paper across her mom's desk without a word.

Her mom read it, then read it again, then looked up with the expression of someone who has just discovered the key has been under the gutter the whole time. Lily leaned back in the office chair. "Pick a good one," she said. "Something long and weird, like RubberDuckPolymer42. I'll wait."

activity: to explain why ancient Egyptians built the pyramids and how the Nile shaped their farming
knowledge_domain: to explain why ancient Egyptians built the pyramids and how the Nile shaped their farming
fact: The main grain crops of ancient Egypt were emmer wheat and barley, used to make the bread and beer that were everyday food for most people.
story:
Jasmine had built the Nile in a baking tray, and tonight it was going to flood whether it wanted to or not. Tomorrow she had to explain the pyramids to her whole class, and Mr. Chaudhry had said her first draft sounded like she'd copied it off a cereal box. "Why did they build them there, Jasmine? That's the question," he'd said. She still didn't have an answer, so she'd filled one side of the tray with sand, pressed wooden blocks into it, and dribbled water from a jug along the other side. Victoria sat cross-legged on the kitchen floor, guarding the pretzels.

"Watch," Jasmine said, and poured slowly. The water spread sideways into the low sand, leaving a dark, wet smear. She poked it. Silt. Muddy, crumbly, perfect-looking dirt. "The Nile did this every year. Flood, then mud, then they could farm right beside a desert." She set a small dish of flour in the wet stripe and another dish in the dry sand far from the water. Victoria leaned in, chewing. "So the river chose where they lived," she said. "And the pyramids are just up on the high dry ground, out of the flood." Jasmine felt the answer click into place like a locker. "Built on the edge, close enough to load stone blocks on boats, far enough to stay dry. That's why there."

Then Victoria asked the question Jasmine dreaded. "Okay, but what did they actually grow in that mud? For the quiz part?" Jasmine froze. She had a page of notes from the museum trip, somewhere. She dug through her backpack while Victoria read the flour packet as if it might confess. Corn? Rice? The water dripped off the tray edge onto the floor, tick, tick, tick. Finally Jasmine found the crumpled page, the one she'd written beside the display of three-thousand-year-old loaves, where Mavrik had asked the guide the same thing.

"Emmer wheat and barley," she read aloud. "They used them to make the bread and beer that were everyday food for most people." Victoria blinked. "Beer? For kids?" "It was food, basically. It says the loaves in the case were authentic, real ones, preserved." Victoria pointed at the wet tray. "And every loaf started with a flood like that one. That's your whole talk, Jaz." Jasmine copied the two grain names onto an index card and stood it beside the wooden blocks, then poured the last of the jug so the little river flooded again, right on cue.

activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
knowledge_domain: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
fact: Correlation does not prove causation: two things rising together, like ice cream sales and sunburns, may both be caused by something else, such as hot weather.
story:
Hayden was standing in line at the pharmacy with his mom's prescription slip in one hand and four dollars and a dream in the other. The dream was the chocolate on rack three. Between him and rack three stood a display of vitamin gummies shaped like dinosaurs, with a sign in aggressive red letters: KIDS WHO TAKE THESE SCORE HIGHER ON TESTS.

Nayla poked his shoulder. She and Yan had come in for bus passes. "You should get those," she said. "It says right there. Higher on tests."

"It says kids who take them score higher," Hayden said. "It doesn't say the gummies do it."

Yan picked up a bottle and read the back. "My cousin takes these. He also has a math tutor, a laptop, and a dad who quizzes him at dinner. He'd score higher on cardboard."

"That's not fair," Nayla said. "Maybe it's both."

The line moved, so Hayden moved with it, still thinking. Mr. Schneider was at the counter, sliding a white bag toward an old man and saying something about taking it with food. Hayden had known Mr. Schneider since second grade, when Hayden had come in weekly for penny candy and Mr. Schneider had never once raised the price.

"Mr. Schneider," Hayden said when it was his turn, handing over the slip. "That sign. If kids who take the gummies score higher, doesn't that mean the gummies work?"

Mr. Schneider typed something into the computer. "Here's one," he said, not looking up. "Ice cream sales go up in summer. Sunburns go up in summer too. Do you think the ice cream is burning people?"

"No. It's just hot out."

"There you go, then." He stapled the bag. "Two things rising together, and something else is doing the lifting."

Hayden stood there a second longer than necessary. He was thinking about who actually buys dinosaur gummies: parents with money to spare, the same parents who buy tutors and breakfast and quiet rooms to study in. He couldn't see any of that in the sign. The sign only showed the two things side by side, the gummies and the grades, and let you fill in the middle yourself. It was almost clever, in a way he did not appreciate.

"So what would prove it?" Nayla asked, following him toward the exit. "Like an actual test?"

"Take a hundred kids," Yan said, holding the door. "Give half gummies and half nothing, don't tell anyone which is which, and see what happens."

"Nobody's going to fund that," Hayden said.

"I would. For a scholarship, I'd fund anything."

Outside, the summer heat hit them like a wall, and across the street the ice cream truck was already playing its song for a line of sunburned kids.

Hayden pointed. "See?"

"Don't say it," Yan said.

activity: to understand the changes of puberty and why daily showers and deodorant matter
knowledge_domain: to understand the changes of puberty and why daily showers and deodorant matter
fact: Deodorants do not stop sweat; they fight odor by slowing the growth of skin bacteria and covering smells with fragrance.
story:
Arthur stood at the row of sinks and glared at his damp shirt in the mirror. He had used the deodorant stick every single morning for two weeks, and still, by third period, the gray fabric under his arms came back dark with sweat. He had trusted that stick the way you trust an umbrella, and the umbrella had leaked.

Zoya came in to grab paper towels and caught him holding his arms out like a scarecrow. "You're in the wrong bathroom," she said.

"I know. Nobody's here. Look at this." He pointed at the wet patches. "I put this stuff on every day and it does nothing."

She leaned against the sink and considered it. "Deodorant doesn't stop sweat," she said. "It fights odor by slowing the growth of skin bacteria and covering smells with fragrance. Totally different job."

Arthur turned that over. Sweat, apparently, was just water, and the smell came from something invisible living on his skin, tiny things the deodorant was quietly battling while his shirt went on getting damp. So the stick wasn't broken. He had just given it the wrong mission. He remembered, with a small pang of despair, the day he'd sprinted to gym class without any deodorant at all, back before any of this started, back when being smelly felt like a problem that belonged to older kids. Apparently it had only been dormant, waiting.

The bathroom door swung open again and Simona hurried in, waving a stick of her own. "Trade emergency. Mine smells like a pine forest explosion."

"Pine forest is fine," Arthur said. "Now it just has to hold the bacteria line."

He rolled his sleeves up to his elbows, rinsed his face at the sink, and decided that tomorrow he would bring a spare shirt. The deodorant would handle the smell; the shirt would handle the water. Divided labor. He dried his hands and held the door for Simona.

"Nice arms," Zoya called after him.

"Shut up," he said, grinning all the way down the hall.

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
fact: Watering deeply and less often encourages roots to grow downward, while frequent light sprinkling keeps roots near the surface where soil dries fastest.
story:
Isaac crouched on his apartment balcony with two shoebox planters of bean seeds and a bet on the line. "First planter to sprout wins my dessert for a week," Karl had said at school, and Isaac had shaken on it before he thought it through. Now he set the boxes side by side on the railing shelf, right beside Ms. Wright's geraniums on the next balcony over. He planned to monitor both boxes every single morning, and he had promised Karl a full report by Friday.

"I'm going to water mine a little bit every day," Karl announced when he came over on Saturday, eyeing his box like it might bolt if he blinked. "Plants love water, so more water must be better." Isaac scratched his head. He poured a slow, soaking amount into his own box until water dripped out the drainage holes, then left it alone. Karl raised his eyebrows. "You're going to forget yours and lose," he said.

The seeds sprouted at nearly the same time, two green hooks pushing up on the same Tuesday, and the whole class heard about it from Karl before lunch. Rory came over after school to see, and the three of them measured the seedlings with a ruler, gasping at every new millimeter. For a while both boxes looked like twins. Then the weather report ruined everything: a heat wave was coming, four days of blazing sun, starting Monday. "Four days," Rory said, counting on her fingers. "That's like the tundra getting a heat wave. Nothing survives without a plan."

Monday scorched. Tuesday scorched worse. Karl watered his box twice a day with quick sprinkles from a cup, and his seedlings stood up cheerful each morning. Isaac soaked his box only once, deeply, and by Wednesday he was biting his nails. Karl's plants still looked fine, and the dessert bet hung over Isaac like a storm cloud. But Thursday morning, everything flipped. Karl's seedlings lay flat and crisp, wilted even though he had watered them an hour earlier. Isaac's were drooping a little, but standing.

Isaac knelt down and peeled back the soil at the edge of Karl's box. All the roots were huddled in the top layer, right where the sun had baked the soil dry as toast. He checked his own box, and the roots had pushed straight down, deep, where the soil was still dark and damp. "It's the watering," he said slowly, holding up a root so Karl could see. "Frequent light sprinkling keeps roots near the surface where soil dries fastest, and deep watering less often makes them grow downward." Karl stared at his crispy seedlings, then at Isaac's sturdy green rows.

"So my own watering killed them." Karl groaned and flopped into the balcony chair. Ms. Wright leaned over her railing with a watering can and a smile. "Hot week coming next month too," she said. "Planning to replant, boys?" Karl jumped up so fast the chair rocked. "Isaac, get your seeds. Rory, grab the ruler. We're starting over right now, and this time we keep score of everything, the whole cumulative total, every single day." Isaac was already pulling the seed packet from his back pocket.

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: In March 1933, Joseph Goebbels became head of Nazi Germany's new Reich Ministry of Public Enlightenment and Propaganda.
story:
Maya's phone buzzed against her math notebook. In the class group chat, Jolie had posted a photo of a glittery banner that read, "EVERYONE is getting the new StarSpin fidget ring. Don't be the only one left out!" Below it, Mathys had typed, "ok fine I asked my mom." Three more people typed "same" within a minute.

Maya winced. She had wanted a StarSpin too, until five minutes ago. Now a strange itch of suspicion crawled up the back of her neck. Why did the banner feel like it was pushing her, like a hand between her shoulder blades? She scrolled up and read it again. "Everyone." "Don't be the only one." It wasn't telling her the ring was good. It was telling her she'd be lonely without it.

She flashed back to Tuesday, when Mr. Müller had led their class through the World War II exhibit at the history museum. The room had smelled like old paper and floor wax, and one wall held a row of posters from Nazi Germany, bright colors and bold slogans. Maya had leaned close to a small plaque and read it silently: in March 1933, Joseph Goebbels became head of Nazi Germany's new Reich Ministry of Public Enlightenment and Propaganda. "Propaganda," she had whispered. "So one guy was basically in charge of all the posters?"

"Basically," Jolie had said beside her, chewing her gum. "Creepy, right?"

Now, sitting at her desk, Maya remembered something else from that wall: a poster with a famous athlete's face on it, and another that called enemies "parasites," a word so heavy and ugly it had made her stomach tighten. Loaded words, celebrity faces, "everyone is doing it." She typed into the chat: "Quick test. Count how many selling tricks are in that banner." She posted the banner again and circled three things with her finger on the screenshot: everyone, don't be left out, and the tiny photo of a pop singer wearing the ring.

Mathys replied with a single eye emoji, then: "wait. it's doing the poster stuff."

"Exactly," Maya typed. "Someone built this ad like a trap. Doesn't mean the ring is bad. Just means the ad isn't a reason."

Jolie answered with the thinking emoji, and after a long minute she wrote, "I already ordered mine tho." Then, a second message: "but I'm going to write my essay on those posters for Mr. Müller. Want to be my tutor on this stuff? You actually paid attention."

Maya grinned and typed, "Deal. First lesson: make one coherent sentence about why the banner worked." Downstairs, the front door banged and her mother called her name, so Maya dropped the phone in her pocket, grabbed her jacket, and ran.

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
knowledge_domain: recovering from a cold or flu at home
fact: Soap breaks apart the fatty outer layer that surrounds flu viruses, which is one reason washing with soap removes them better than rinsing with water alone.
story:
The thermometer had read normal for two days straight, so Michael's mother finally trusted him with a mission: walk to the pharmacy on Miller Street, buy two bottles of liquid soap, and be back before his little sister's birthday party started at four. His sister had caught his flu anyway, despite everything, and she had asked him one question last night that he couldn't shake. "Why can't I just rinse my hands with water? It feels clean." He had said "because it isn't," which had not satisfied either of them.

At the pharmacy he found Mathis from homeroom stocking shelves as part of his older brother's weekend job, and he pulled both bottles of soap from the display and then, out of curiosity, a bottle of plain hand sanitizer mist that claimed to work without water. "Party's at four," Michael said, checking his phone. "I have maybe twenty minutes to decide."
