His palms had started to perspire inside his jacket, which he hated, because it reminded him he wasn't fully better.

He reasoned it out in the aisle like a puzzle. Last night, helping with dishes, he had watched a greasy pan: water alone slid right off the buttery film, but one drop of soap lifted the whole layer apart and carried it away. His sister's rinse question had the same shape. The flu virus had a fatty outer layer around it, and soap broke that layer apart. That, he realized, was why washing with soap removed the viruses better than rinsing with water alone. Rinsing just moved them around; soap took them apart. He put the mist bottle back on the shelf.

"You're staring at soap like it's going to talk," Mathis said, wheeling his cart closer. Michael explained the greasy pan and the fatty outer layer, fast, because the clock was real now. Mathis, who had planned to grab the cheapest bottle for his own house, changed his mind on the spot. "My mom rinses everything," he said. "I'm getting the real stuff." The cashier, impartial between the five brands on the counter, rang up Michael's two bottles without a comment.

Outside, the wind smelled like cold rain coming, and Michael ran the last two blocks with the bag swinging against his leg, thinking of his sister's question waiting at home like a wave about to become a tsunami of why, why, why. He burst through the door at 3:52, held up the bottles, and said, "Ask me again. I've got the answer now."

activity: to make a roux and turn it into a smooth cheese sauce without lumps
knowledge_domain: to make a roux and turn it into a smooth cheese sauce without lumps
fact: The darker a roux is cooked, the less it thickens, because browning breaks down the flour's starch.
story:
Penelope had exactly one hour before the tasting table opened at the farmers' market, and the cheese sauce was still thin. Ms. Ba, whose stall sold roasted potatoes with sauce on top, had prescribed the recipe on a card: melt the butter, stir in the flour, cook it, whisk in the milk, add the cheese. Sebastian had made the first batch while Penelope fetched the potatoes, and now the sauce slid off a spoon like flavored milk.

"It's called a roux," Sebastian said, pointing at the butter and flour paste he'd cooked. "I watched mine the whole time. It got nice and brown, like peanut butter. I was proud of it."

Penelope looked at the pan. Her own roux, from a practice batch at home, had stayed pale blond, and that sauce had gone thick enough to cling to a spoon. Sebastian's was much darker and much thinner. Same butter, same flour, same milk. The only thing different was the color. She thought about that while customers began drifting toward the stall, sniffing, waiting. If the darker one was thinner, then the browning itself must be doing something to the flour. She could not see inside the paste, but she could test it.

"We make a new batch and pull it off the heat the second it turns blond," she said. "Not brown. Blond."

They did it together. Butter, flour, whisking, counting, and the moment the paste turned the color of weak tea, Penelope poured in the milk in a slow stream. The sauce tightened around the whisk. When she lifted the whisk, the sauce hung, then fell in a slow ribbon. Sebastian added the cheese a handful at a time, and it melted in smooth, without one lump.

Ms. Ba looked into the pot and started ladling it over potato samples. The line of customers, who had been indifferent to the first thin batch, came back for seconds. "Half the market just voted for your sauce," Ms. Ba said. "That's democracy in action. Blond roux wins by a landslide."

Penelope wrote on the recipe card, in block letters, TAKE IT OFF EARLY, and taped it above the burner.

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: After flying across time zones, the body clock adjusts at an average of about one day for each hour of time difference.
story:
Riley's family had flown six hours of time zones to reach the coast, and they were staying in a small pension two streets back from the beach. On the second night, he lay in the narrow bed with his eyes wide open while the clock on the wall ticked past midnight. His parents were awake too; he could hear them whispering in the next room, and his little sister had come out twice for water.

In the morning, bleary, he walked down to the sand. The beach was almost barren at that hour, just hard, wet sand and a line of seaweed from the tide. Two kids were already there, digging near a rock shelf. The girl, Avianna, said they were hunting for shells before the crowds came. The boy, Winter, wanted to find a whole sand dollar, unbroken, to take home to his grandmother, who was sick and collected them.

"You're up early," Winter said.

"Up late," Riley said. "I slept three hours and then just... woke up. Same yesterday. My whole family is a mess."

Avianna brushed sand off her knees. "We get kids like you here every week. Day two is the worst, then it evens out." She counted on her fingers. "My aunt flew here from six hours away last spring. She was wide awake at midnight on day two, better on day three, and normal by day six. One day awake for every hour of difference, that's what the pattern looked like."

Riley turned that over. Six hours of time zones, six days. He had assumed the tiredness would just fade whenever it felt like fading, but if the pattern held, he could plan around it. If he wanted to be sharp for the boat trip his dad had booked for day four, day four would be a lagging day, but the last day, day six, would be a good one.

That night he set his notebook by the bed and wrote the numbers down. When he woke at two in the morning, he did not fight it. He read by the window, then went back to sleep, and in the morning he felt half human. He decided to test it properly: he would save the long coastal hike and the snorkeling for days five and six, and let his sister have the boring museum on the tired days.

He found Winter at the rock shelf at noon, holding something flat and white.

"Is it whole?" Riley asked.

Winter turned it over. Five slots, not a crack anywhere. He wrapped it in his shirt and held it against his chest. "Grandma's going to lose her mind."

activity: going on a school field trip with the class
knowledge_domain: going on a school field trip with the class
fact: A dairy cow only produces milk after she has given birth to a calf.
story:
The bus smelled like hay and banana sandwiches, and James pressed his forehead to the window the whole way so he wouldn't miss the moment the fences started. Behind him, Loic was arguing with Eugene about whether farms still used horses. "Nobody uses horses," Eugene insisted. "Everything's machines now." James wondered about that. He had never been to a farm, so anything seemed possible to him.

Their teacher, Ms. Farah-Ali, handed out clipboards at the gate. "We're at a dairy farm," she said, "so pay attention to how the pieces fit together. Ask the people who work here; they know how the whole system is governed, from grass to fridge." James liked the word governed. It made the farm sound like a small country.

In the milking barn, James counted the cows in the stalls. Twelve of them stood patiently while machines hummed and milked them, and a woman in rubber boots moved down the row, checking each one. Loic leaned over to James. "Weird question," he whispered. "Why don't they just keep milking the same cow forever? Like a juice box that never runs out."

James started to say that seemed right, but then he noticed something. Every single cow in the barn had a small ear tag, and beside each stall, on a whiteboard, the workers had written two dates. He stood on tiptoe and squinted. Both dates on every line, not just some of them. He tugged the worker's sleeve. "What are those two numbers for?" She smiled. "First is when she had her calf. Second is when she started milking. Every girl in this barn has had a baby." James felt the thought click into place like a puzzle piece he'd been holding upside down. So it wasn't like a juice box at all. A cow gives milk only after she has had a calf, which meant every cow here was a mother. He turned to Loic. "Your juice box idea is wrong. They all had calves first. That's the rule."

Outside, the March wind cut through James's jacket until they reached the calf pens, where the deep straw worked like insulation and the air felt warm and sleepy. A calf with velvety ears nuzzled Eugene's hand, and Eugene, who had been so certain about machines, went quiet for a long moment. "Okay," he said finally, "the machines do the milking. But the calves do everything else." James watched the calf blink its enormous eyes and thought how strange and wonderful it was that all that milk in the barn began here, in a wobbly-legged animal smaller than his desk. When Ms. Farah-Ali called them back, James was still looking at the calf. "See you soon, I guess," he told it.

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: Historians still do not know who fired the first shot at Lexington in April 1775; British and colonial witnesses each said the other side fired first.
story:
Rachel slid two photocopies across the dinner table, one in each hand, like she was dealing cards. "Dad, you're a British soldier. Mom, you're a colonial militiaman. Read your page out loud."

Her dad set down his fork. "This is for history club? I thought you and Solomon had it finished."

"We did. Then Mr. González gave us two eyewitness accounts from Lexington, April 1775, and told us we present tomorrow morning." She tapped the pages. "Now read. Please. I recruited you two because Solomon's family is busy and Bryce's family just argues about whose turn it is to do dishes."

Her mother cleared her throat and read. "He says a British officer shouted, the colonials scattered, and a shot came from behind a wall. So the colonials fired first."

Her dad frowned at his own page. "My guy says he heard the colonials yell like Indians and then saw the smoke come from the colonial line before any British musket went off."

"Exactly!" Rachel jumped up so fast her knee knocked the table. "They were standing on the same road on the same morning, and they each swear the other side fired first."

"That's impossible," her dad said. "Somebody had to shoot first."

"That's what I thought. I asked Mr. González after school, and he said no. Historians still don't know who fired that first shot. Nobody does. Both sides said the other side did it, and nobody can prove either one."

Her mother leaned back, chewing slowly. "So your presentation is going to be 'we don't know'?"

"It's going to be 'how can we not know.'" Rachel pulled a notepad from her backpack and scribbled while she talked. "I tested it. I asked Solomon and Bryce about the fight in the cafeteria last week, the one where the tray went flying. Solomon swore Bryce's friend started it. Bryce swore it was the other kid. Both of them honest. Both of them sure." She circled a line she'd written: eyewitnesses can be certain and still opposite. "That's my whole argument. If two people can see one tray crash differently, imagine a smoky road at dawn with muskets going off."

She copied the sentence onto a fresh index card, then held it up so her parents could read it. Her dad read it, nodded, and pointed his fork at her plate.

"Eat first," he said. "Your potatoes are getting cold, and your big moment is imminent."

Rachel stuffed the card in her pocket, still chewing.

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: A primary source is a firsthand record from the time, such as a letter, photograph or official data, and it is often the best place to check a claim.
story:
At 7:42 on a Tuesday night, Marcus's phone buzzed with the group chat. Gurleen had posted a photo of the plaque in Riverside Park: "FOUNDED 1821 BY EZRA HALE, HERO OF THE VALLEY." Under it she wrote, "For my history poster. Done!" Then Abbey typed, "My grandpa says Ezra Hale was a fraud. He says Hale stole the land and the 1821 thing is a lie." Gurleen replied with three angry face emojis and the words, "Are you implying my poster should say FRAUD on it?"

Marcus stared at the screen. One of them had to be wrong, and both of them sounded completely sure. He remembered a book report from last fall where he had written that a dinosaur was extinct in Australia, and Mr. Novák had written "check this" in red pen, and it had turned out Marcus had copied the mistake from a website that copied it from another website. He had never forgotten how that felt. He typed, "Everybody relax. Grandpa's story and the plaque are both just things people say. I'll check for real."

The next afternoon he rode his bike to the library, where Mr. Novák was shelving DVDs near the local history room. Marcus explained the argument, and Mr. Novák smiled and led him to a tall cabinet of crumbling old newspapers and a box of letters with faded ink. "These are what I'd call a primary source," Mr. Novák said, pulling on white gloves. "A firsthand record from the time, like a letter, a photograph, official data. Often the best place to check a claim." He laid out a land register from the 1820s and a letter written in a looping hand.

Marcus worked through the register line by line until his eyes ached. There it was, in brown ink: Ezra Hale's name on a deed dated 1821, alongside a sale recorded to the original farming family, with a fair price listed beside it. The letter, from one of the farmers, grumbled about taxes but mentioned "Hale keeping his word on the bridge money." No fraud. Marcus photographed the pages, and his hands were shaking a little as he did it, though he wasn't sure whether that was triumph or something else.

That night the chat lit up. Marcus posted the photos, then wrote, "Checked the original land register and a letter from 1822. Hale bought the land fair, founded the town in 1821, paid for the bridge. The plaque checks out." Gurleen sent a crown emoji. Abbey typed for a long time; the little dots appeared and vanished twice before her message came through: "Okay. I'll tell Grandpa the letter beats his story. He's going to sulk like the antagonist in my novel." Marcus grinned and started typing back, "Tell him the farmers in the letters sulked too," and then, before he could send it, Abbey added, "Bring the photos Monday? I want to see Hale's actual signature."

"Front page of my poster," Marcus replied.

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: Glittering generalities are vague, positive words like "freedom" or "natural" that make people feel good about something without saying anything specific or checkable.
story:
Ariana flopped into the seat beside Carolina as the bus lurched away from the school stop. In her backpack was the granola bar her mother had bought because the box said "pure, natural goodness" in letters bigger than the name of the product. Ariana had wanted to like it, and instead she'd spent all of science class feeling tricked. Now she pulled the box out and held it up in front of the ad plastered across the bus ceiling, which showed a famous singer holding the same bar. "Nine out of ten kids agree," the ad said underneath.

"That's weird," Carolina said, leaning over. "Nine out of ten kids can't agree on anything. Not even what pizza to order." Ariana started counting on her fingers. "Pure. Natural. Goodness. Those are all nice words, but the box doesn't actually say anything with them. Watch." She flipped the box over and read the small print. The second ingredient was something called "chocolate-flavored coating," and further down was a word so long she had to sound it out in pieces. "So it says natural on the front, and on the back it's stuff like that."

The bus swayed through another stop, and Ariana pulled a pen from her pocket and began a diligent little survey, scribbling on the back of her homework sheet. Every ad on the bus got two columns: "nice-sounding words" and "things I could actually check." The sneaker ad had "everybody's wearing them," which wasn't checkable either, unless she counted shoes, which she did, at the next stop, out the window. Four sneakers, three of them a different brand. The "everybody" claim started to wobble right there.

"Ms. Ionescu calls those glittering generalities," Carolina said, peering at the list. "Vague positive words. She had it on a poster." Ariana grinned and circled her three columns of them. "Monday, I'm bringing this box to class," she said. "Front and back." She held it up to the window where the afternoon light caught the shiny letters, then turned it over and tapped the tiny ingredient list. "This side's the honest one."

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
fact: Frost-tender crops such as tomatoes, peppers and squash are planted outdoors only after the last spring frost, because freezing temperatures kill them.
story:
Abigail counted the pots on her apartment balcony for the third time, as if the number might change. Six tomato seedlings, four peppers, two little squash plants that had just unfurled their first true leaves. "Fine," she muttered. "Census complete. Twelve citizens of Plant Village."

Her phone buzzed. It was Aspen, texting from two floors down: FROST WARNING TONIGHT. GET YOUR BABIES INSIDE.

Abigail stared at the screen. Frost. She flashed back to the Saturday three weeks ago when she and Suri had carried the seedling trays up from the hardware store, proud as anything. Suri had squinted at the little plastic markers and said, "It says plant after the last frost. What frost? It's practically summer." Abigail had waved her off. The sun was warm, the balcony was bright, and waiting felt like something boring people did. They had planted everything that same afternoon, then eaten popsicles on the railing like farmers celebrating a harvest that didn't exist yet.

Now she crouched beside the tomatoes and tried to think like a detective. The leaves looked fine, green and perky, so the cold hadn't come yet. But the warning said it would arrive overnight, and overnight was only about nine hours away. She needed an objective answer to one question: would the temperature on her balcony actually drop below freezing? The balcony faced east and sat above the parking lot, so maybe it stayed a touch warmer than the ground. But "maybe" wasn't good enough. Freezing temperatures killed plants like these. Tomatoes, peppers, squash, all of them, gone black and limp by morning.

She knocked on the door across the hall before she could talk herself out of it. Mr. Littlechild opened it holding a mug that said WORLD'S OKAYEST GOLFER. "Mr. Littlechild, do you have a thermometer I could borrow? Mine only goes on my forehead."

He raised an eyebrow. "Frost night, is it? My knees said so this morning." He dug out an old outdoor thermometer shaped like a frog and handed it over. "Bring it back alive."

By seven, the reading on the balcony read four degrees, and it was still dropping. That settled it. She couldn't gamble on the bricks holding heat until dawn. Abigail lined up the pots along the kitchen floor, moving the watering can and a stack of library books to make room. When Aspen knocked, she was carrying a sled full of old towels, which was the silliest thing Abigail had seen all week, and they both cracked up in the doorway.

"It's not for the plants," Aspen said, wiping her eyes. "It's for sliding the pots over. Suri's bringing the wagon for the squash. She's taking the stairs because the elevator smells like someone's burnt soup."

They worked in a chain, pot to towel to wagon, until Plant Village was resettled by the living room window like refugees at a very sunny resort. At midnight Abigail woke and padded out to check the thermometer frog, which now read minus one. In the morning the balcony railing wore a thin white crust, and her breath came out in little ghosts.

She knocked on the door across the hall again, holding the frog thermometer and a paper plate stacked with toast. "Your thermometer survived," she announced. "The tomato citizens thank you."

Mr. Littlechild took the plate and studied the frost sparkling on her balcony rail. "Smart girl. Next spring, wait for the last frost before you plant."

"Next spring," Abigail said, "I'm making Plant Village a calendar."

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: Yellowstone became the first national park in the United States on March 1, 1872, when President Ulysses S. Grant signed it into law.
story:
Cameron had wanted this beach trip for one reason: the junior ranger program at the state park next to the shore, which ended with a quiz and a real badge. He had brought his notebook to the sandcastle contest that afternoon, but instead of helping Eleanor and Malakai replicate the lighthouse they had built last summer, he sat on a towel memorizing facts about sea turtles and sand crabs. Eleanor wanted to win the contest, and she told him so twice.

"You're copying last year's tower wrong," she said, jabbing a finger at their lopsided pile. "The wall goes around the moat, not through it. And sea turtles are herbivores mostly, right? Then come dig."

Cameron dug. The sand smelled like wet pennies, and the wind kept blowing grit between his teeth. He had a theory about the quiz: the ranger, Mr. Traoré, would ask the same number of questions every year, and the last one would be the hardest, something no kid at the beach could know, because it would be about a park far away. It seemed arbitrary, but the pattern held in the two old programs Cameron had found in the nature center binder.

That evening the campfire crackled near the dunes, and Mr. Traoré held up a pinecone for the microphone. He asked about tides, about the sea turtle's diet, about what a herbivore eats. Kids shouted answers. Then came the last question, and the whole crowd of parents and kids went quiet. "Which park became the first national park in the United States, and when?"

Nobody raised a hand. Cameron's father scratched his head. Malakai whispered, "Yosemite?" and got a shake of the head from Eleanor.

"Yellowstone," Cameron said, standing up. "It became the first national park in the United States on March 1, 1872, when President Ulysses S. Grant signed it into law."

Mr. Traoré smiled and pinned the badge to Cameron's shirt. Eleanor pushed through the crowd, holding a blue ribbon from the contest. "We got second," she said. "Because the wall finally went around the moat. You want to see it before the tide takes it?"

Cameron ran down the dark beach with her, badge glinting under the lantern light, straight toward the lighthouse of sand.

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: Demand for necessities, such as essential medicines, changes little when their price changes; economists call this inelastic demand.
story:
Jordan had exactly eleven dollars and forty minutes before his mom picked him up, and the garage sale on Marlow Street was already crowded. He pushed past a rack of coats to the card table, where Ms. Harper, his neighbor, was sorting a shoebox of basketball cards. Right on top sat a Kenyon rookie card, the one Jordan had wanted since Peyton got his for a birthday. The sticker said two dollars.

Then a man in a Celtics cap stopped, picked up the card, and asked if she had more. Behind him, another collector appeared, and a third. Within five minutes they were offering each other money, and Ms. Harper, who had looked up Kenyon's card on her phone, quietly crossed out the sticker and wrote twenty dollars. Jordan's stomach dropped. Twenty dollars, because there was only one and three people wanted it. Meanwhile, a whole crate of ordinary cards sat marked one dollar for the entire box, and nobody even glanced at it.

"Can I help?" Jordan asked. Ms. Harper smiled and put him in charge of the board games, which had not sold at three dollars each. Jordan advocated dropping them to fifty cents, and Ms. Harper agreed to try it. The games sold four in a row, so he marked the mountain of plush toys at a quarter, and those went too. Plenty of something, low price; one of something everybody wanted, high price. It was almost like a rule, and he kept testing it in his head as he made change.

At the table, the Celtics cap guy was still holding Kenyon. "My wife thinks I'm crazy," he told Ms. Harper. "Same with her sister and that allergy medicine." Ms. Harper nodded. "My EpiPen went up again this year, almost double what it used to be, and I still buy two every time." The man frowned. "That doesn't follow. Everything else here got cheaper when nobody wanted it." Jordan drifted closer, pretending to straighten a stack of comics.

"How come you don't just skip it?" he asked. "When nobody wanted those games, we had to lower the price or they'd never sell." Ms. Harper turned the EpiPen box she'd bought for herself, one she kept in her purse, over in her hands. "Because after my diagnosis last spring, the doctor said I can't be without it. My pharmacist calls that inelastic demand." She said it lightly, the way you'd say any ordinary thing, and picked up her price marker.

Jordan looked at the Kenyon card, then at his eleven dollars, and made a decision. He tapped the Celtics cap guy's arm. "There's another rookie card at the sale two blocks over," he said. "My friend Walid texted me. Want me to run and check before you pay twenty?" The man handed him a five for the trouble, and Jordan sprinted down Marlow Street, feeling buoyant, Walid's address glowing on his phone screen.

activity: to explain the phases of the Moon by modelling it circling Earth with a lamp and a ball
knowledge_domain: to explain the phases of the Moon by modelling it circling Earth with a lamp and a ball
fact: The Moon spins once for each trip around Earth, so the same side always faces us.
story:
Emma's bedroom looked like a crime scene involving a lamp, a basketball, and an orange. "You said this would take ten minutes," said Benny, who had been recruited on the promise of leftover pizza.

"It will, once I figure out why the Moon's face never changes." Ms. Crowchild had assigned them a project: explain the phases of the Moon to the class using a model. Emma had the lamp on her desk, the ball as the Moon, and the orange as Earth, because the basketball would not fit on the shelf she needed it on. The setup was diagonal across the room, which meant she kept tripping over the cord.

She walked the basketball around the orange, watching the shadow slide across its surface. Half lit, then a crescent from this angle, then full. That part worked. But something bothered her, and it had bothered her since Tuesday, when she'd lain on the trampoline with her dad and noticed the dark patches on the Moon made the same lopsided face they always made. "It's like the Moon is posing," she had said. "Same profile every time." Her dad had shrugged and said the Moon wasn't very adventurous.

"Okay, watch," she told Benny. "If the Moon always shows us the same face, it can't just float around us facing one fixed direction." She marked a smiley face on the basketball with a pencil, held it so the face pointed at the orange, and started around the orbit. Halfway, the smiley face pointed at the wall. "See? Wrong. It would show us its back."

"So turn it."

"No, I have to keep turning it the whole way." She shuffled in a slow circle, rotating the ball a bit with every step so the face stayed aimed at the orange. When she completed the trip, the face had come back around to where it started. She counted the turns in her head: exactly one spin for one trip around.

"So it turns," said Benny, "but never shows its other side. Rude."

"It spins once for each trip around Earth," Emma said. "That's why the same side always faces us."

Benny leaned over to study the smiley face. "Can I draw a back side? Maybe a mustache."

Emma handed him the pencil. "Elaborate all you want. Nobody down here will ever see it."

He drew the mustache anyway, grinning, while the lamp threw a perfect crescent across the basketball.
